lessons.title: Boolean Logic and Truth Tables
lessons.description: NOT, AND, OR and XOR gates, truth tables up to three inputs, and Boolean expressions.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Boolean Logic?

Boolean logic underpins all digital computing. Inside a processor, every decision reduces to combinations of 1s and 0s. Logic gates are the physical building blocks that implement Boolean operations in hardware — they take binary inputs and produce a binary output according to a defined rule.

You must know four logic gates for your exam: NOT, AND, OR and XOR. A truth table is the standard way to show how any gate or combination of gates behaves — it lists every possible set of input values and the resulting output.

The Four Logic Gates

The NOT gate has a single input and inverts it. If the input is 1, the output is 0; if the input is 0, the output is 1. It is sometimes called an inverter. In Boolean notation, NOT A is written with an overbar: Â.

The AND gate outputs 1 only when every input is 1. If any input is 0, the output is 0. In Boolean notation, A AND B is written as A · B (a dot). Think of it as: both conditions must be true.

The OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. It outputs 0 only when every input is 0. In Boolean notation, A OR B is written as A + B (a plus sign). Think of it as: at least one condition is true.

The XOR gate (exclusive OR) outputs 1 when exactly one of its inputs is 1 — but not when both are 1. This is what makes XOR different from OR: OR is true when one OR both inputs are true; XOR is true when one input is true but NOT both. In Boolean notation, A XOR B is written as A ⊕ B.

Key Fact

XOR outputs 1 only when inputs differ (one is 0, the other is 1). When both inputs are the same (both 0 or both 1), XOR outputs 0. This is the key distinction from OR, which outputs 1 when both inputs are 1.

NOT (single input):
A=0 → Output=1  |  A=1 → Output=0

AND:
A=0, B=0 → 0  |  A=0, B=1 → 0  |  A=1, B=0 → 0  |  A=1, B=1 → 1

OR:
A=0, B=0 → 0  |  A=0, B=1 → 1  |  A=1, B=0 → 1  |  A=1, B=1 → 1

XOR:
A=0, B=0 → 0  |  A=0, B=1 → 1  |  A=1, B=0 → 1  |  A=1, B=1 → 0

The XOR row is the one to practise. AND and OR are more intuitive; XOR’s A=1,B=1 → 0 is the row students most often get wrong.

Boolean Notation

Your exam uses a specific set of symbols for Boolean expressions. You must recognise and use them correctly:

  • A · B means A AND B (a dot between variables).
  • A + B means A OR B (a plus sign between variables).
  • A ⊕ B means A XOR B (a circled plus sign).
  • Â (A with an overbar above it) means NOT A.

So the expression (A AND B) OR (NOT C) is written as: A · B + Ç. Always evaluate brackets first, just as in ordinary arithmetic.

Truth Tables with Three Inputs

When a circuit has three inputs (A, B, C), the truth table needs 23 = 8 rows to cover every combination. List the input columns in a consistent binary counting pattern so no combination is missed:

Expression: (A AND B) OR (NOT C) — written as A · B + Ç

Add an intermediate column for A · B, then a column for NOT C, then combine with OR for the final output.

Row 1: A=0,B=0,C=0 — A·B=0, NOT C=1, Output=1
Row 2: A=0,B=0,C=1 — A·B=0, NOT C=0, Output=0
Row 3: A=0,B=1,C=0 — A·B=0, NOT C=1, Output=1
Row 4: A=0,B=1,C=1 — A·B=0, NOT C=0, Output=0
Row 5: A=1,B=0,C=0 — A·B=0, NOT C=1, Output=1
Row 6: A=1,B=0,C=1 — A·B=0, NOT C=0, Output=0
Row 7: A=1,B=1,C=0 — A·B=1, NOT C=1, Output=1
Row 8: A=1,B=1,C=1 — A·B=1, NOT C=0, Output=1

Notice that adding intermediate columns makes it straightforward to avoid errors. The output is 0 only when A·B=0 AND C=1 (rows 2, 4, 6).

Key Fact

A truth table for n inputs has 2n rows. Two inputs: 4 rows. Three inputs: 8 rows. Always list input combinations in binary counting order (000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111) to guarantee every combination is covered. Add intermediate columns for complex expressions.

Logic Circuits and Expressions

A logic circuit diagram shows gates connected by wires. Your exam may ask you to convert between a Boolean expression and a circuit diagram, or to complete a truth table for a given circuit. Work methodically: label the output of each gate as an intermediate value, then trace each row of the truth table through the circuit gate by gate.

Conversely, given a circuit diagram, write the expression by reading the gates from inputs to output. The output of each gate becomes the input expression for the next. Brackets group gates that feed into a later gate. This skill requires practise — draw example circuits and write their expressions until the pattern becomes automatic.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Boolean logic questions typically appear as 2–6 marks. For truth tables, always add intermediate columns for sub-expressions in brackets before filling in the final output column — this prevents cascading errors. XOR is the gate students most often confuse with OR: remember, XOR outputs 0 when both inputs are 1. For three-input tables, write all 8 input rows in binary counting order first (000 to 111) before filling any outputs. For expression-to-circuit questions, draw each gate in the order you would evaluate the expression (innermost brackets first). The Boolean notation · for AND, + for OR, ⊕ for XOR, and overbar for NOT will appear in questions — make sure you recognise each symbol instantly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four gates to know: NOT (inverts input), AND (output 1 when all inputs are 1), OR (output 1 when any input is 1), XOR (output 1 when exactly one input is 1 — not both). XOR’s A=1, B=1 → 0 is the critical distinction from OR.
  • Boolean notation: A · B = AND, A + B = OR, A ⊕ B = XOR, overbar = NOT. Always evaluate brackets first. A three-input truth table needs 8 rows (23).
  • Add intermediate columns when completing truth tables for combined expressions, and work through each row systematically to avoid errors.

lessons.title: CPU Architecture and the Fetch-Execute Cycle
lessons.description: The ALU, control unit, clock, bus and registers — and how the CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the CPU?

The CPU is the component that carries out every instruction a program contains. It processes data, performs calculations, makes comparisons and controls the flow of information between all other parts of the system. Without the CPU, no program can run.

Most CPUs follow the design principles of Von Neumann architecture, named after the mathematician John von Neumann whose work in the 1940s described storing both instructions and data in the same memory. This is the foundation of the vast majority of computers made since then, from desktop PCs to smartphones.

Key Fact

The main components inside the CPU are: the ALU (performs arithmetic and logic operations), the control unit (directs data flow and manages the fetch-execute cycle), the clock (generates timing pulses), registers (small, fast storage locations inside the CPU) and the bus (a collection of wires for transmitting signals between components).

Inside the CPU: Key Components

The ALU carries out two categories of operation. Arithmetic operations include addition, subtraction and related calculations. Logical operations include comparisons (is A greater than B?) and Boolean operations (AND, OR, NOT). Every time an app performs a maths calculation, checks a condition in a loop, or compares two values, the ALU is doing the work.

The control unit does not process data itself. Instead, it orchestrates everything else — sending control signals to tell the ALU to start calculating, telling memory to send data, and directing results to the right place. It decodes each instruction and determines which components need to act and in what order.

The clock generates a continuous stream of pulses. Each pulse triggers the next step in a process. The faster the clock, the more operations the CPU can perform per second. Modern consumer CPUs typically operate at several gigahertz — billions of clock pulses per second.

Registers are tiny storage areas built directly into the CPU. They hold data or addresses that the CPU is currently working with. Because they are physically on the processor chip itself, registers can be accessed far faster than main memory. You do not need to know the names of individual registers for this course.

A bus is a set of parallel wires that carry signals between parts of the system. Different buses carry different types of information: data, addresses and control signals. Data travels along the bus in parallel, with each wire carrying one bit at a time.

Cache sits between the CPU and main memory (RAM). When the CPU needs data, it checks the cache first. If the data is there (a “cache hit”), it is retrieved much faster than fetching from RAM. If not (a “cache miss”), the CPU fetches from RAM and copies the data to cache for next time. Cache is much more expensive per byte than RAM, so systems have relatively small amounts of it — typically measured in megabytes. Many modern CPUs have multiple levels of cache (L1, L2, L3), each larger but slightly slower than the last.

The Fetch-Execute Cycle

The CPU works by repeating the same three-stage process continuously for every instruction in a program. This is the fetch-execute cycle:

1. Fetch — The next instruction is retrieved from main memory and brought into the CPU. The CPU knows where to look because it tracks which instruction comes next. The instruction travels to the CPU along the data bus.

2. Decode — The control unit interprets the instruction to work out what operation is needed and what data is required. Different instructions require different actions — the control unit figures out which components need to be involved and what they must do.

3. Execute — The instruction is carried out. This might mean the ALU performs a calculation, data is moved between memory locations, or the result is written back to main memory. Once execution is complete, the cycle repeats for the next instruction.

This cycle repeats billions of times per second in a modern processor. A common exam error is writing only two stages (“fetch and execute”). There are always three stages: fetch, decode and execute. The decode stage is separate and must be stated.

Key Fact

The fetch-execute cycle has three stages: Fetch (instruction retrieved from memory), Decode (control unit interprets what the instruction means), Execute (instruction is carried out, which may include reading or writing to main memory). This repeats for every instruction.

CPU Performance Factors

Three factors have the greatest effect on how fast a CPU can process instructions:

Clock speed — measured in hertz (Hz), typically gigahertz (GHz) in modern CPUs. A higher clock speed means more fetch-execute cycles per second. Doubling the clock speed roughly doubles the number of instructions the CPU processes per second, all else being equal.

Number of cores — a core is an independent processing unit. A dual-core CPU has two cores; a quad-core has four. Multiple cores allow the CPU to work on different tasks simultaneously (parallel processing). Modern phones and computers typically have 4 to 16 cores. More cores improve performance for programmes written to take advantage of them.

Cache size — a larger cache stores more frequently used data closer to the CPU, reducing the number of slower RAM accesses needed. Applications that repeatedly access the same data (such as games or video editing) benefit most from larger cache.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam mistake is describing the fetch-execute cycle as two stages. There are always three: fetch, decode, execute — and the decode stage is what the control unit does, not the ALU. When asked to “explain the effect of increasing clock speed on CPU performance”, always link back to the fetch-execute cycle: “a faster clock means more fetch-execute cycles per second, so more instructions are processed per second.” For questions about CPU components, distinguish clearly between what the ALU does (arithmetic and logic) and what the control unit does (directs data flow, manages the cycle) — they are different components with different roles. You do not need to know the names of specific registers (such as MAR, MDR, PC or CIR) for this course.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The CPU contains the ALU (calculations and logic), control unit (directs activity and manages the cycle), clock (timing pulses), registers (fast on-chip storage) and buses (wires for signal transmission). Most CPUs follow Von Neumann architecture: instructions and data share the same memory.
  • The fetch-execute cycle has three stages: Fetch (instruction retrieved from memory), Decode (control unit interprets it), Execute (action carried out). This repeats continuously for every instruction.
  • CPU performance is affected by clock speed (cycles per second), number of cores (parallel processing) and cache size (faster access to frequently used data). Increasing any of these generally improves performance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the control unit within the CPU.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks for: the control unit manages/coordinates the fetch-execute cycle; it directs the flow of data between the CPU, memory and input/output devices (or: it sends control signals to other components to tell them what to do and when).
One mark for: identifies the control unit as a managing/coordinating component without explaining what it manages.

practice_questions.text: Describe the three stages of the fetch-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three stages clearly described with accurate detail. Fetch — instruction retrieved from main memory and brought into the CPU. Decode — control unit interprets the instruction to determine what action is needed. Execute — the instruction is carried out (e.g. ALU performs calculation, data is written to memory). Cycle repeats for the next instruction.
Secure: All three stages named and described but one stage lacks detail.
Developing: Two stages described correctly.
Emerging: One stage described, or all three named but with no description.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the number of processor cores can improve computer performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple cores allow different instructions or tasks to be processed simultaneously (parallel processing). If a program is written to use multiple cores, different parts of the program can execute at the same time, reducing overall execution time. Links to real-world context (e.g. video editing, multitasking).
Secure: States that multiple cores allow simultaneous processing and that this speeds up overall performance.
Developing: States that more cores = faster performance but gives no mechanism.
Emerging: Vague statement that more cores is better.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between the ALU and the control unit.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations / control unit directs data flow and manages the fetch-execute cycle; ALU processes data / control unit sends control signals without processing data; ALU carries out calculations / control unit decodes instructions.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of increasing cache size on CPU performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A larger cache means more frequently used instructions and data can be stored closer to the CPU. The CPU checks cache before RAM; if data is in cache (cache hit), it is retrieved much faster than from RAM. More cache means fewer slower RAM accesses (fewer cache misses), reducing the time the CPU spends waiting for data. Overall processing speed increases for data-intensive tasks.
Secure: States that more cache reduces the number of times the CPU needs to access RAM and that this is faster.
Developing: States that more cache improves speed but does not explain why (cache vs RAM speed difference).
Emerging: Vague reference to cache being fast.

glossary_terms.definition: Central Processing Unit — the primary component of a computer that processes instructions and coordinates the operation of all other components.
A computer architecture in which both program instructions and data are stored in the same memory and accessed through a single pathway.
Arithmetic Logic Unit — the part of the CPU that performs arithmetic calculations and logical comparisons.
The part of the CPU that manages and coordinates all activity, directing data between the CPU, memory and input/output devices.
A component that generates regular electrical pulses to synchronise the activities of the CPU. Clock speed is measured in hertz (Hz).
Small, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU used to temporarily hold data and instructions being processed.
A collection of wires along which data or signals are transmitted between components inside a computer system.
The continuous three-stage process by which the CPU processes instructions: fetch (retrieve from memory), decode (interpret the instruction) and execute (carry it out).
A small amount of very fast memory located on or very close to the CPU, used to store frequently accessed instructions and data.

lessons.title: Memory and Storage
lessons.description: RAM, ROM, cache, registers, volatile vs non-volatile, secondary storage types and cloud storage.
lessons.content_html:
Primary and Secondary Storage

Computers use two broad categories of storage. Primary storage (also called main memory) is directly accessible by the CPU and is used for data and instructions the computer is currently working with. Secondary storage is separate from main memory and holds data long-term, even when the power is off. The CPU cannot access secondary storage directly — data must first be loaded into primary storage before the CPU can process it.

Key Fact

The four types of primary storage are: RAM (main working memory, volatile), ROM (startup instructions, non-volatile), cache (fast small memory on or near the CPU) and registers (the fastest storage, inside the CPU itself). RAM and ROM are the two you will be asked to compare most often.

Volatile and Non-Volatile Memory

A critical distinction in storage is whether memory retains its contents without power. Volatile memory is erased when power is cut. Non-volatile memory keeps its contents without power. RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile. This is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut — it exists only in volatile RAM.

RAM — Random Access Memory

RAM is the computer’s main working memory. When you open an application, the operating system copies it from secondary storage into RAM so the CPU can access it quickly. RAM is much faster than any form of secondary storage but loses everything when the computer is switched off.

The amount of RAM affects how many programs can be open at once without slowing down. A computer with more RAM can hold more data in quick-access memory, reducing the need to fetch from slower secondary storage. Modern computers typically have between 8 and 64 GB of RAM.

ROM — Read Only Memory

ROM stores the firmware instructions that run when the computer first powers on. These instructions initialise the hardware and begin loading the operating system from secondary storage into RAM. ROM is non-volatile and read-only in normal use, so its contents cannot be accidentally overwritten.

ROM is much smaller than RAM — it needs to hold only the minimal startup code, not entire programs. A computer’s ROM might contain just a few megabytes, whereas RAM is measured in gigabytes.

RAM: Volatile (loses contents without power)  |  Read and write  |  Stores currently running programs and data  |  Typically 8–64 GB in modern systems  |  Contents change constantly during use.

ROM: Non-volatile (retains contents without power)  |  Read-only in normal use  |  Stores startup firmware/boot instructions  |  Very small (typically a few MB)  |  Contents are fixed at manufacture.

Why Is Secondary Storage Needed?

Secondary storage is essential because RAM is volatile — switch the computer off and all RAM contents are gone. Secondary storage provides three things that primary storage cannot: persistence (files survive when power is off), capacity (far more data can be stored, measured in terabytes) and portability (storage devices can be moved between computers).

Every file you save, every application installed, and the operating system itself live on secondary storage. When you open a file, it is copied from secondary storage into RAM. When you save, it is written back from RAM to secondary storage.

Key Fact

Secondary storage is needed for three reasons: capacity (far more data than RAM can hold), persistence (data is retained without power) and portability (storage devices can be transported and used in other systems). RAM is fast but temporary; secondary storage is slower but permanent.

Types of Secondary Storage

Magnetic storage uses magnetic fields to encode data on a surface. Hard disk drives (HDDs) store data on rapidly spinning metal platters coated with a magnetic material. A read/write head moves across the spinning surface to access or record data. Magnetic tape is an older form used for archival backup — sequential access makes it slow to retrieve specific files but it can store very large amounts at low cost.

Solid-state storage (SSD) stores data in electronic memory chips with no moving parts. Because nothing physically moves, SSDs are faster, quieter, lighter and more shock-resistant than HDDs. However, SSDs cost more per gigabyte of capacity. Smartphones, tablets and modern laptops commonly use SSDs.

SSD advantages: Faster access times (no moving parts to position), silent, uses less power, more durable (resistant to physical shock), lighter and more compact.

SSD disadvantages: More expensive per GB, capacity per pound spent is lower than HDD, limited write cycles (though this is not a practical issue for typical usage).

HDD advantages: Lower cost per GB, available in very large capacities (multiple TB), widely available.

HDD disadvantages: Slower access (mechanical parts must physically move to the right position), produces heat and noise, vulnerable to physical shock (head crash), heavier and larger.

Cloud Storage

Cloud storage means storing files on servers owned and managed by a third party, accessed over the internet. Services such as these are used by millions of people and businesses to back up files, share data across devices and collaborate remotely.

Advantages of cloud storage: Files are accessible from any device with internet access, data is backed up automatically (protection against local hardware failure), easy to share files with others, and no physical hardware to manage or replace.

Disadvantages of cloud storage: Requires an internet connection to access files, dependent on the service provider remaining operational, raises privacy concerns (data is held by a third party), and ongoing subscription costs can be higher long-term than purchasing local storage. Access can be slower than local storage if internet speeds are limited.
lessons.exam_tip_html: RAM vs ROM comparison questions are extremely common. Make sure you know the key contrast: RAM is volatile and read/write; ROM is non-volatile and read-only. For secondary storage questions, you must be able to explain the operation of both solid-state and magnetic storage and compare their advantages and disadvantages — not just name them. For cloud storage, always give both sides when asked to “discuss” or “evaluate”: accessibility and automatic backup are advantages; internet dependency, privacy concerns and cost are disadvantages. When a question asks why secondary storage is needed, use the three-word answer: capacity, persistence, portability.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary storage: RAM (volatile, holds current programs and data), ROM (non-volatile, holds startup firmware), cache (fast, close to CPU) and registers (fastest, inside CPU). Secondary storage provides capacity, persistence and portability that RAM cannot.
  • Secondary storage types: magnetic (HDDs and tape — moving parts, cheaper per GB, slower); solid-state (no moving parts, faster, more expensive per GB, durable). Both have distinct trade-offs.
  • Cloud storage stores files on remote servers accessed over the internet. Advantages include any-device access and automatic backup; disadvantages include internet dependency, privacy concerns and subscription costs.

practice_questions.text: Explain why secondary storage is needed in a computer system.

Mastering: Explains that RAM is volatile (loses contents when power is removed), so secondary storage is needed to retain data and programs permanently. Also explains that secondary storage provides far greater capacity than RAM and that storage devices can be portable. Ideally uses the terms capacity, persistence and portability.
Secure: States that data must be saved permanently because RAM loses its contents, and gives one other reason (capacity or portability).
Developing: States that secondary storage keeps data when the computer is off but gives no further reasoning.
Emerging: Vague reference to saving files or storage.

practice_questions.text: Compare solid-state storage with magnetic hard disk storage. In your answer, include one advantage of each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Solid-state has no moving parts so is faster, quieter, more durable and uses less power. Magnetic HDD is cheaper per GB and available in larger capacities. Comparison structured directly (e.g. 'SSDs are faster than HDDs because they have no moving parts to position'). Both advantages and a direct comparison.
Secure: One advantage of each type stated correctly with direct comparison of at least one feature.
Developing: One advantage of one type stated with some comparison attempt.
Emerging: Names both types but comparison is vague.

practice_questions.text: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of using cloud storage instead of a local hard drive.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two advantages (e.g. files accessible from any device / automatic backup protects against local hardware failure / easy to share files / no physical hardware to manage). One disadvantage (e.g. requires internet connection / privacy concerns as data held by third party / ongoing subscription cost / potentially slower access). All points explained, not just listed.
Secure: Two advantages and one disadvantage stated with brief explanation.
Developing: One advantage and one disadvantage stated.
Emerging: One point stated.

practice_questions.text: Explain why cache memory improves CPU performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cache is faster to access than RAM because it is closer to (or on) the CPU. The CPU checks cache before accessing RAM. If frequently used data is in cache (cache hit), retrieval is much faster than a RAM access. More cache means more data can be held close to the CPU, reducing the number of slower RAM accesses (cache misses). Result: less time waiting for data.
Secure: States cache is faster than RAM and that frequently used data is stored there.
Developing: States cache is fast but does not explain why it reduces RAM accesses.
Emerging: Vague reference to cache being close to the CPU.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
A) ROM
B) RAM
C) Secondary storage
D) Cache on a USB drive
practice_questions.marks: B) RAM [1 mark]

glossary_terms.definition: Memory that the CPU can access directly, including RAM, ROM, cache and registers. Also called main memory.
Persistent storage separate from main memory, used to store files, programs and operating systems when the computer is not actively using them.
Memory that loses all its stored data when the power supply is switched off.
Memory that retains its stored data even when the power supply is switched off.
Random Access Memory — volatile primary storage that holds the programs and data the CPU is currently using. Its contents are lost when power is removed.
Read Only Memory — non-volatile primary storage that contains the startup instructions (firmware) needed to initialise the computer. Its contents cannot be changed by normal programs.
Storage that uses magnetic fields to record data on spinning platters (HDD) or magnetic tape. Data is encoded as north/south magnetic poles.
Storage that uses electronic flash memory chips with no moving parts. Data is stored as electrical charges in floating-gate transistors.
Storing data on remote servers accessed over the internet, rather than on local hardware.

lessons.title: Software, Programming Languages and Translators
lessons.description: System vs application software, low- vs high-level languages, and compilers, interpreters and assemblers.
lessons.content_html:
Hardware and Software

Hardware is the physical equipment that makes up a computer. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. Neither is useful without the other: the most powerful processor in the world does nothing without software to direct it, and the cleverest program needs hardware to run on.

Key Fact

All software falls into one of two categories: system software, which manages the computer’s resources and provides a platform for other software to run, and application software, which performs tasks directly for the end user.

System Software

System software sits between the hardware and the user. It handles the low-level work that applications rely on. The three main types are the operating system, utility programs, and device drivers.

An operating system (OS) manages five key areas: the processor (deciding which programs get CPU time), memory (allocating RAM to programs as they open), input/output devices (communicating with keyboards, screens, printers), applications (providing services applications need, such as file access), and security (managing user accounts and access permissions). Without the OS, every application would need to include its own code for all of these — an impossible duplication of effort.

Utility programs carry out maintenance tasks. A file compression tool reduces the size of files before they are transferred; a disk cleanup tool removes temporary files to free up space; encryption software scrambles data so it cannot be read if intercepted. These are distinct from applications because they serve the system itself rather than the user’s primary tasks.

Application Software

Application software is what most people think of when they think of a program: a web browser, a word processor, a banking app, a game. Applications depend entirely on system software — they request services from the OS rather than communicating with hardware directly. This separation keeps development manageable: a game developer writes code to draw a window and play sound, and the OS handles the rest.

A common exam error is to describe an antivirus program as application software. It is a utility (system software) because its purpose is to maintain the health of the system, not to help the user complete a personal task. Similarly, a device driver is system software — the user never directly interacts with it, but the OS uses it to communicate with a printer or graphics card. Application software, by contrast, is always directly task-facing: photo editing, messaging, spreadsheets.

Programming Languages: Low-Level and High-Level

Processors can only execute instructions written in machine code — patterns of 0s and 1s. Writing in machine code directly is extremely difficult and error-prone. Programming languages were developed to give programmers a more human-readable way to express instructions.

Low-level languages are close to the hardware. They offer fine control over exactly how the processor operates, but they are difficult to read, write, and maintain. High-level languages use English-like syntax, hide the complexity of the hardware, and can run on many different types of processor without modification.

Key Fact

High-level languages are easier to write and debug, portable across hardware, and closer to natural language. Low-level languages give precise hardware control and can produce faster, more efficient code, but they are harder to write and specific to one processor type.

Machine Code and Assembly Language

Machine code is the only language a processor can execute directly. It is expressed entirely in binary and is specific to a processor or family of processors — code written for one architecture will not run on a different one without modification.

Assembly language replaces raw binary with short, memorable codes called mnemonics (for example, MOV to move data, ADD to add two values). Each line of assembly corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction — this is called a 1:1 correspondence. Assembly language is still tightly bound to the processor’s architecture and is most commonly used when developing software for embedded systems or when direct control over specific hardware is needed.

Translators: Compiler, Interpreter, Assembler

Because processors only understand machine code, any program written in a high-level or assembly language must be translated before it can run. There are three types of translator: the compiler, the interpreter, and the assembler.

A compiler reads the entire source code of a program and translates it all into machine code at once. The output is an executable file that can be run as many times as needed without the compiler being present. Errors are only reported after the whole program has been analysed, which makes them easier to review together. Once compiled, the program runs quickly because no further translation is needed at run time.

An interpreter translates and executes a program one line at a time. It does not produce a standalone machine code file; instead, it calls appropriate machine code subroutines within its own code to carry out each statement. If the program encounters an error mid-way, it stops at that line — making it easier to spot exactly where a mistake occurred. The downside is that the interpreter must be present every time the program runs, and execution is generally slower because translation happens at run time.

An assembler converts assembly language into machine code. Because each assembly mnemonic maps directly to one machine code instruction (the 1:1 correspondence), this translation is straightforward. Like a compiler, an assembler translates its input into machine code directly — the output is machine code that the processor can execute.

Key distinction for your exam: both assemblers and compilers translate their input directly into machine code. Interpreters do not generate machine code directly — they call machine code subroutines to carry out each statement.

Most modern high-level languages are typically run using an interpreter during development (easier debugging, immediate feedback) and compiled for the final product (faster execution, no dependency on the interpreter). Some languages use a combination of both approaches, compiling to an intermediate form before interpreting.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In ‘compare and contrast’ questions on compilers and interpreters, make sure you address both speed and error-reporting in a single structured paragraph rather than listing features of each separately. A common error is to say interpreters “produce machine code line by line” — they do not produce machine code at all; they call machine code subroutines. Also remember that assemblers and compilers both translate directly to machine code, while interpreters work differently. When explaining system vs application software, always link to function: system software manages resources, application software performs user tasks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • System software (OS, utilities, drivers) manages hardware resources and provides a platform for applications. Application software performs end-user tasks and relies on the OS.
  • Low-level languages (machine code, assembly) are close to the hardware and processor-specific. High-level languages (such as Python) are portable and easier to write.
  • Compilers and assemblers translate source code directly into machine code; interpreters call machine code subroutines to execute programs line by line without producing a standalone executable.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes system software?
A) Software that performs tasks directly for the end user
B) Software that manages computer hardware resources and provides services for applications
C) Software that is downloaded from the internet
D) Software that can only run on one type of processor
practice_questions.marks: B) Software that manages computer hardware resources and provides services for applications [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two functions of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: managing the processor / managing memory / managing I/O devices / managing applications / managing security. [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a precise functional difference, e.g. a compiler translates the entire program into machine code before execution, producing a standalone executable; an interpreter translates and executes one line at a time without producing an executable.
Secure: Correctly contrasts one aspect (e.g. compiler produces machine code file / interpreter does not) with some supporting detail.
Developing: Vague contrast attempted (e.g. one is faster) without explaining why.
Emerging: Names compiler and interpreter without comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between low-level and high-level programming languages.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two well-explained differences, e.g. (1) High-level languages use English-like syntax and are portable across different processors, whereas low-level languages are specific to a processor's instruction set. (2) High-level languages are easier to read and maintain; low-level languages give precise hardware control and can produce faster, more efficient programs.
Secure: Two differences identified with some development.
Developing: One clear difference with basic explanation, or two differences without development.
Emerging: Simple differences listed with little or no explanation. [2 marks per difference]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the '1:1 correspondence' between assembly language and machine code.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that each assembly language instruction (mnemonic) maps to exactly one machine code instruction, so the assembler replaces each mnemonic with its binary equivalent — no compression or expansion of code occurs. Links to why assembly is still low-level (no abstraction).
Secure: States that one assembly instruction produces one machine code instruction, with an example or brief expansion.
Developing: States the 1:1 relationship without explaining its implications.
Emerging: Vague reference to assembly and machine code being related. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare compilers and interpreters as methods of translating high-level language programs into machine code. In your answer, refer to how each translator works, the type of output produced, and how errors are reported.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Structured comparison covering all three areas: (1) A compiler translates the whole program at once; an interpreter translates one line at a time, calling machine code subroutines. (2) A compiler produces a standalone executable; an interpreter produces no permanent machine code file. (3) A compiler reports all errors after full analysis; an interpreter stops at the first error it encounters. Evaluates appropriateness (compiler better for finished software; interpreter better for development/debugging).
Secure: Addresses two of the three areas with accurate comparisons.
Developing: Some accurate points made but comparison structure weak or one area missing.
Emerging: Describes one translator only, or highly confused distinctions. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of software manages hardware resources and provides a platform for applications to run?
An assembler and a compiler both translate source code directly into machine code. Which statement correctly describes what an interpreter does instead?
options: It translates the whole program into machine code before execution
It calls machine code subroutines to carry out each statement without producing machine code directly
It converts assembly mnemonics into binary at a 1:1 ratio
It produces a standalone executable that runs without the interpreter

knowledge_checks.q: Assembly language has a _____ correspondence with machine code, meaning each assembly instruction maps to exactly one machine code instruction.
A _____ translates an entire high-level program into machine code at once and produces a standalone executable file.
Match each translator to its description:
right: Translates the whole program into machine code, producing a standalone executable
Translates and executes a program one line at a time, calling machine code subroutines
Converts assembly language mnemonics into machine code at a 1:1 ratio

glossary_terms.definition: Physical components of a computer system that you can touch, such as the processor, memory, keyboard and monitor.
A set of instructions that tells hardware what to do. Software cannot be touched — it exists as data stored on hardware.
Software that manages computer system resources and provides a platform on which application software can run. Examples include operating systems and utility programs.
A type of system software that manages hardware resources and provides services for application software. Examples include Windows, macOS, iOS and Android.
Software designed to perform specific tasks for the end user, such as a word processor, web browser, or game.
Binary instructions that can be executed directly by a processor. Each type of processor has its own specific machine code instruction set.
Programming languages that are close to machine code, offering little or no abstraction from the hardware. Includes machine code and assembly language.
Languages that use English-like syntax, are portable across different processors, and are much easier to read and write than low-level languages. Examples include Python and Java.

A low-level language that uses short mnemonics (like MOV, ADD, SUB) to represent machine code instructions. It has a 1:1 correspondence with machine code: each assembly instruction maps to exactly one machine code instruction.
A translator that converts an entire high-level language program into machine code in one go, producing a standalone executable file.
A translator that converts and executes a high-level language program one line at a time, without producing a standalone executable. The interpreter must be present every time the program runs.
A translator that converts assembly language into machine code. Because there is a 1:1 correspondence, each assembly instruction produces exactly one machine code instruction.
